I got into Tech/IT in the 1990's and got out a few years ago. It's a field that's FAR too fractured these days and I'm afraid you will kill your passion. Entry level will be phone support, listening to people bitch and moan in some cubicle farm with ungodly high turn-over. Expect to spend a year or two there before being able to move up (assuming you don't get any sort of certs/degree). You might luck into something else, but phone support is the biggest entry level option.

When I needed a break I went from Tech to motorcycle mechanics, which was my passion. I completely and utterly murdered that passion. Burned it to the ground and then salted the Earth where it once stood so Nothing could rise from that spot again. Yup, it was that bad. I am a Firm proponent of the belief that if you turn your passion into work that you will kill it.

If you want to do something different, find something that Interests you, that you Like but aren't passionate about. That's what Tech was to me, something I liked, had fun with, but never loved. If I had need to find a job, I'd be looking at a trade like Electrician. You get to work indoors, in the dry, and it's something EVERYONE needs. Having been involved with multi-million dollar commercial building projects, the general contractor was forever bitching about his subs not showing up, being locked up (Monday mornings were the worst) or just being worthless sacks of shit. Be a warm body with even a smattering of work ethics and you'll be forever in demand.

But that's just my take....

As someone who worked for 12 years, professionally, and longer out of passion, doing computer service and who now works installing security systems and cameras, my advice to you is to choose a profession where you have something constructive to show for yourself at the end of the day. I'm finding the system installation side of things fulfilling in a way that computers alone never really reached.

Do you like to travel? Can you turn a wrench (just barely)

If so, service tech for industrial equipment.

Equipment is getting and being designed so complicated that no generalist mechanic can deal with some of its quirks. So the manufacturer makes tons of money sending out service techs to do the repairs. Its kinda like arduino stuff, except vastly more complicated. You get travel provided by your employer, and a low hours work week that pays damn good, and if you become really good you can sometimes make your own service business. But dont worry if you arent that good, they have a special phone number and a special manual just for you so that you can fix things that we cannot.

Downsides, Dealing with jerks demanding you show up yesterday, and fix major breakages in 5 seconds, because their machine is down and it costs then $XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX per hour of downtime. Very odd hours, this is not a day job or an office job, if a machine is down and the part isnt coming in until 9pm, you will go chill at the hotel and come back when the part does, working into the early morning.

And if you decide you are done with the job, maintenance technicians with electrical knowledge are in demand almost everywhere, with experience you can command a day shift position and work something resembling a 9-5.

I dont do it, but I have itchy feet and an office job in which I hire these guys, I am so jealous.

Nobody will hire you to do programming unless you have a degree (doesn't have to be in computer science though) or you are a savant.

Other than that I have no tips. A shorter bit of training might get you something on the hardware side of computers. Training to do some trade is also widely recommended. An electrician of some sort may help lead you back to computers if that is what you want to do.
